newsitem.title: USA: House turns back campaign fundraising measure.
newsitem.headline: House turns back campaign fundraising measure.

text.p: In a stunning rebuke to House Republican leaders, lawmakers Thursday turned back a bill to provide millions of dollars for a wide-ranging investigation of White House fundraising problems.

Despite a day of frantic lobbying by Republican leaders, 11 members of their own party voted against a procedural motion needed to bring a committee funding bill to the House floor. It was defeated 213-210.

Conservative Republicans said they voted against the bill because it would have increased overall spending for congressional committees by 14 percent at a time when lawmakers have promised to balance the budget.
"I'm not going to leave here this weekend with a sick feeling in my gut that I voted to increase spending," said Representative Mark Neumann, a Wisconsin Republican.
After the vote, Republicans quickly called a private meeting to try to figure out how to proceed on the politically sensitive issue.

The legislation would have allocated funding for House committees during this session of Congress. It included a 50 percent increase in funding for the Government Reform and Oversight Committee, which is spearheading the investigation of possible Democratic fundraising abuses in the 1996 campaign.

Democrats charged the bill would have provided $12-15 million, or more, to the committee for what they termed a partisan witch hunt into White House fundraising problems -- while ignoring congressional fundraising abuses.

The bill set aside $3.8 million for the investigation. Democrats said the real price tag was much higher in part because Republicans had created a separate $8 million fund the committee could dip into if needed.

"Today the majority is crossing the line. They are trying to jam a funding bill through ... and they are authorising an investigation that is limited to Democrats," said California Democratic Representative Henry Waxman. "That can't be interpreted as anything other than a coverup."
A Senate committee has launched its own $4.3 million investigation of possible campaign fundraising problems.

Democrats also charged that committee chairman Dan Burton, a conservative Indiana Republican, was running the panel with a heavy hand and had sent out subpoenas without consulting Democrats. Burton defended his work on the House floor.

"I've been accused of some things, I think unfairly, but I expected that to happen. When you start investigating the executive branch of government that involves the president, you've got to expect they're going to fight back," he said.
Burton said the committee would carry out the investigation in a fair, evenhanded manner. He said congressional fundraising violations should be turned over to the ethics committee.
Burton become become embroiled in a fundraising controversy of his own this week, when a former lobbyist for Pakistan accused Burton of shaking him down for donations.

The brouhaha came during debate on what is normally a sleepy bill to fund congressional committees. It is the latest in a host of problems that have beset congressional Republicans as they prepare to investigate Democratic fundraising.
Senate Republican leaders were also rebuffed in their initial efforts to secure funding for an investigation.

Florida Republican Representative Porter Goss said the defeat was "Pretty much a money issue. I don't think it is a big setback at all for the leaders, it was a procedural vote with a lot of issues intertwined in it."
Asked if some Republicans were concerned about Burton's leadership, he said there may be some members who question him, in what he said were "cloakroom whispers."

Some Republican moderates want the scope of the investigation widened. A Justice Department task force is also investigating questionable foreign and other funds given to Democrats that might violate U.S. campaign laws.
